title: Presentation Skills for B1–B2

pts: Presentations require sustained, planned, one-directional speech without the turn-taking support of conversation.
This demands different preparation and different classroom practice from the interactive tasks Tier II otherwise emphasises.
Neither skill set substitutes for the other — both deserve dedicated attention.

v: Two short recordings or live demonstrations

items: Two colleagues (or two learners) talk about the same topic for two minutes as a conversation.
One of them then gives a two-minute talk on the same topic to the group.
The group notes differences: sentence length, pauses, connectors, planning, eye contact.
Discuss what learners need to learn for each mode.
Plan a week that includes both dialogic and monologic speaking.
Transcribe thirty seconds of each and compare the language directly.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: Did you go to the Dasara exhibition?
B: Yeah, on Sunday. So crowded!
A: What did you see?
B: Mostly the stalls… and the palace lights.
Today I’d like to tell you about the Dasara exhibition in Mysuru. I’ll talk about its history, what you can see there, and some tips for visiting. First, the history…

blocks.x: The monologue has longer sentences, explicit structure and no partner to share the work. Neither mode replaces the other.

body: Purpose: to show the difference between dialogic and monologic speech. Content: two panels. On the left, two players hitting a ball back and forth, labelled ‘Conversation’. On the right, a single musician performing a solo to an audience, labelled ‘Presentation’. Style: clean, energetic. Board version: two stick-figure panels.

items: A phone voice recorder app (free) for the two recordings.

blocks.x: A live demonstration by the teacher and a volunteer.

points.sub: A genre with its own moves
pts: Presentations follow a recognisable genre structure — introduction, body, conclusion, with signposting throughout.
This applies Unit 33's genre-analysis approach directly to spoken, monologic discourse.
Explicit teaching of signposting language ('firstly,' 'to sum up') supports listeners as much as it structures the speaker.

v: A model presentation transcript (written for this book)

items: Learners listen to or read a short model presentation.
They identify the introduction, main points and conclusion.
They underline the signposting phrases.
Sort the phrases into a table: opening, sequencing, moving on, giving examples, concluding.
Learners plan a two-minute talk using at least one phrase from each row.
Remove all signposts from a transcript; learners put them back.
Support: provide the table with phrases already sorted.
Challenge: learners add phrases for referring back (As I mentioned earlier…).

lines: Opening: Good morning. Today I’m going to talk about…
Outline: I’ll cover three points: first…, then…, and finally…
Moving on: Now let’s turn to… That brings me to my second point.
Example: For instance… A good example of this is…
Concluding: To sum up… So, the main points are… Thank you for listening.

blocks.x: Signposts help listeners, who cannot reread a spoken text, as much as they help the speaker stay organized. This is the genre approach of Unit 33 applied to monologue.

body: Purpose: to show signposting. Content: a winding road through a landscape with signboards at each turn: ‘Today I’ll talk about…’, ‘First…’, ‘Moving on…’, ‘To sum up…’. A listener in a car follows easily. Style: bright, map-like. Board version: a road with four signs.

items: Quizlet (free basic version) for signposting phrase sets.

blocks.x: A signposting poster on the classroom wall.

points.h: Visual Aids as Support, Not a Script
pts: Visual aids should support key points, not carry full sentences the presenter then simply reads aloud.
Over-reliance on text-heavy slides undermines fluency practice by turning presentation into reading practice instead.
Teach this distinction explicitly — it's a common default habit worth deliberately unlearning.

v: Two sample slides; chart paper or slide software

items: Show two slides on the same point: one full of sentences, one with a picture and a few key words.
Learners watch a short talk using each slide and say which was easier to follow, and why.
Discuss what happens when the speaker reads the slide.
Learners redesign a text-heavy slide from their own work.
Practise presenting from the redesigned slide without reading.
‘Picture only’ challenge: each slide contains only an image and a heading.
Support: allow small cue cards with key words.
Challenge: no notes at all; the slide is the only prompt.

lines: Plastic waste is a major problem in Indian cities because it blocks drains, causes flooding during the monsoon, harms animals such as cows that eat it, and takes hundreds of years to break down.
Heading: Plastic in our cities. Image: a blocked drain. Key words: drains, floods, animals, slow to decay.

blocks.x: If learners read full sentences from a slide, the presentation becomes a reading-aloud exercise, not speaking practice.

body: Purpose: to contrast two slides. Content: two projector screens. The left is crowded with small text, and the presenter faces the screen with her back to the audience. The right shows one image and three words, and the presenter faces the audience. Style: clear contrast. Board version: two rectangles, one full of lines, one with a drawing.

items: Google Slides (free) or Canva for Education (free for teachers) for slide redesign.

blocks.x: Chart-paper posters with a drawing and three key words.

body: Give learners a simple rule: no sentence on a slide that you will also say aloud. Headings, images, numbers and key words are fine.

pts: Public monologic speech often triggers more anxiety than paired conversation, connecting directly to Unit 22's affective factors.
Low-stakes practice presentations to a single partner before a full-class version build confidence incrementally.
Frame early attempts explicitly as low-stakes practice, not performance, to reduce anxiety's impact on language production.

items: Learners present a one-minute talk to a single partner.
They present the same talk to a group of three, with one improvement.
They present again to a group of six.
Only after these rounds do volunteers present to the whole class.
Call the first rounds ‘rehearsals’; tell learners they are not being marked.
The 4/3/2 technique: learners give the same talk three times to new partners in four, three and then two minutes (Nation and Newton 2009).
Support: learners may keep a cue card for the first two rounds.
Challenge: add a question from the audience in each round.

lines: Today is practice. No marks. The only goal is to get to the end of your talk. If you stop, smile and continue.
First time I forgot everything after one sentence. Third time I didn’t need my card.

blocks.x: Repetition builds fluency, and each wider audience is a small, manageable step up in pressure. This applies the self-efficacy principle of Unit 22: confidence grows from actual success.

body: Purpose: to show graded exposure. Content: a learner at the centre of three widening circles: one partner, a small group, a whole class. Her posture becomes more confident in each circle. Style: warm, encouraging. Board version: three circles.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version) for round timers.

blocks.x: The teacher claps to signal the end of each round.

points.sub: The dialogic moment within a monologue
pts: A question-and-answer segment turns a monologic presentation briefly dialogic, demanding a different, less-planned skill.
Teach specific language for clarifying a question, buying thinking time, and handling a question without a ready answer.
This connects to Unit 27's strategic competence, applied to a genuinely high-pressure spoken moment.

items: Teach three groups of phrases: clarifying, buying time, and handling an unknown answer.
Pairs practise: A reads a question card; B answers using a phrase from each group where possible.
Learners give a short talk, then take two questions from the audience.
The audience is given question stems in advance so that questions come quickly.
Debrief: which phrases helped?
‘Hot seat’: one learner answers rapid questions on a topic they know well.
Support: questions written in advance and given to the presenter.
Challenge: unexpected questions, including a challenging one.

lines: Clarifying: Sorry, do you mean…? Could you repeat the question?
Buying time: That’s an interesting question. Let me think for a moment.
Unknown answer: I’m not sure, but I think… I’ll find out and tell you tomorrow.
S1: Why did you choose this topic?
S2: Good question. Let me think… I chose it because my grandfather is a farmer in Mandya.

blocks.x: These are strategic competence moves (Unit 27): ways to keep communication going under pressure.

body: Purpose: to show strategies for questions. Content: a presenter in water holding a question mark, with three lifebuoys labelled ‘Clarify’, ‘Buy time’ and ‘Be honest’ floating within reach. Style: friendly, slightly humorous. Board version: three circles with labels.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for audience questions submitted anonymously.

blocks.x: Question slips passed forward to the presenter.

pts: Give peers specific, structured criteria to give feedback against, rather than an open 'what did you think?'
This connects to the collaborative-assessment principles developed fully in Unit 43.
Specific criteria also give the listening audience a genuine purpose, rather than passive attendance.

blocks.x: Two stars and a wish, with criteria

items: Share three or four criteria before any presentations.
Assign each listener one criterion to focus on.
After each presentation, listeners complete a slip: two strengths and one suggestion, linked to their criterion.
Presenters read the slips and choose one suggestion to act on.
The teacher reviews a sample of slips for quality.
Group feedback: listeners with the same criterion agree on one comment together.
Support: provide comment starters.
Challenge: listeners must quote something the presenter said.

lines: Structure: clear introduction, main points and conclusion.
Signposting: phrases that guide listeners.
Delivery: eye contact, pace, volume.
Visuals: support, not script.
Criterion: Signposting. Star: ‘That brings me to my second point’ was very clear. Star: good summary at the end. Wish: say how many points at the start.

blocks.x: Specific criteria give the audience a listening purpose. Unit 43 develops peer feedback and collaborative assessment fully.

body: Purpose: to show structured peer feedback. Content: a presenter at the front; in the audience, learners hold cards labelled with different criteria and write notes. Style: clean, engaged. Board version: four criteria written as column headings.

items: Google Forms (free) for peer feedback forms.

blocks.x: Peer feedback slips, collected in an envelope for each presenter.

pts: Shorter presentation lengths and more visible structural scaffolding (sentence starters, a fixed outline) support lower-level learners.
This connects to Unit 15's differentiation principles, applied specifically to a demanding, high-exposure task type.
Build toward longer, less scaffolded presentations progressively across a course, not as a single fixed format.

v: A fixed outline with sentence starters

items: Give lower B1 learners a fixed outline with sentence starters for each part.
Set a short target: one to two minutes, three main sentences.
Learners complete the outline in writing, then practise aloud in pairs.
Over the term, remove starters one at a time and lengthen the target.
Keep a record of each learner’s level of support.
Picture-based presentations: learners talk about three photos in order.
Support: a fully completed model, which learners adapt by changing details.
Challenge: learners choose their own structure after the first term.

lines: Hello. My name is… Today I will talk about…
First,… Second,… Finally,…
To sum up,… Thank you. Any questions?
Weeks 1–3: full frame, one minute. Weeks 4–6: frame without middle starters, two minutes. Weeks 7–10: outline headings only, three minutes.

blocks.x: This is differentiation (Unit 15) and scaffolding that is gradually withdrawn.

body: Purpose: to show fading support. Content: three pictures of a building. In the first, it is covered in scaffolding; in the second, some scaffolding has been removed; in the third, it stands alone. Labels read ‘Full frame’, ‘Partial frame’, ‘Own structure’. Style: architectural, clear. Board version: three simple buildings.

items: Google Docs (free) for editable outline templates.

body: Giving learners even a short planning time before speaking can make a measurable difference. In a well-known study, learners who planned before a task produced more fluent and more complex speech than those who did not (Foster and Skehan 1996). For presentations, planning time is not a luxury but part of the task.

pts: Recording a presentation and reviewing it afterward builds self-awareness that live delivery alone rarely provides.
This connects to Unit 19's self-study strategy training, applied to a specific, high-value reflective technique.
Frame self-review around specific criteria, not general self-criticism, to protect the affective safety of the exercise.

items: Learners record a two-minute presentation on a phone (their own or a shared class phone), with consent.
They watch or listen to it once for general impressions.
They watch again with a checklist of four criteria.
They note one strength and one goal.
They re-record after practice and compare the two versions.
Audio only for learners uncomfortable on camera.
Support: a checklist with three items only.
Challenge: learners transcribe thirty seconds and note hesitations and self-corrections.

lines: Did I introduce my topic and main points? Did I use signposts? Did I look up from my notes? Was my speed comfortable for listeners?
Strength: clear conclusion. Goal: I said ‘um’ many times before each point. Next time I will pause instead.

blocks.x: Frame self-review around criteria, not general self-criticism (I sound terrible). This extends the self-study strategies of Unit 19 and links to the portfolio work in Unit 42.

body: Purpose: to show structured self-review. Content: a learner looking at a phone screen that shows herself presenting; beside it, a checklist with ticks. Her expression is thoughtful, not anxious. Style: calm, reflective. Board version: a phone outline and a four-item checklist.

items: A phone camera or voice recorder app (free).
Audacity (free, open source) for audio playback and trimming.

blocks.x: A peer watches and fills in the checklist on the presenter’s behalf.

body: Ask your class to give the same one-minute talk three times to three different partners this week. Record one learner’s first and third attempts, with permission, and compare them. Most teachers hear a clear gain in fluency.

dek: Unit 40 of 100: extended, planned monologic speech is a distinct skill from the dialogic focus of most classroom talk — and one many intermediate learners need explicit support with.

aims.x: This unit turns from dialogue to monologue. Presentations ask learners to plan and deliver extended speech to an audience, without the turn-by-turn support of conversation. Many intermediate learners find this hard, and many classrooms give it little systematic practice. The unit shows how to teach presentation as a genre and a skill, and how to build confidence step by step.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain how monologic speech differs from dialogic speech;
teach presentation structure and signposting language;
guide learners to use visual aids as support rather than script;
reduce presentation anxiety through staged, low-stakes practice;
teach strategies for handling audience questions;
organize structured peer feedback on presentations;
scaffold presentations for lower B1 learners and reduce support over time;
use recording and criteria-based self-review.

why: Why this matters. Most classroom speaking practice is dialogic — conversation, discussion, negotiation. Sustained monologue demands a different, often under-practised set of skills.

background.x: In conversation, speakers share the work. A listener nods, asks a question or finishes a sentence, and each turn is short. In a presentation, one speaker carries the whole load: planning content, organizing it, choosing words and producing them fluently, all while monitoring the audience. Levelt’s (1989) model of speech production describes three linked processes: conceptualizing what to say, formulating it in words and grammar, and articulating it. In monologue, all three run continuously with no partner to buy time. Goh and Burns (2012) therefore treat extended speaking as a skill that needs its own teaching, including the planning and self-regulation strategies that support it.

Planning helps. Research on task planning found that when learners had time to prepare, their speech tended to become more fluent and more complex (Foster and Skehan 1996), which connects with the balance of fluency, accuracy and complexity in Unit 29. Presentations are a genre with recognizable stages (Swales 1990; Unit 33), and signposting language helps both speaker and listener to follow those stages. Visual aids can help too, but only if used well: Mayer’s (2009) research on multimedia learning suggests that people understand better when words are spoken alongside relevant images than when the same words are also printed in full on the screen. A slide crowded with text competes with the speaker instead of supporting her.

In Indian schools and colleges, presentations are increasingly common: project presentations, seminar papers, science exhibitions, morning assembly talks and, later, job and university interviews. Yet many learners meet them without preparation, write a script, memorize it and deliver it at speed while looking at the floor. Presentation anxiety is real and often intense (Unit 22), especially where English is linked to social judgement. The NCF 2023 calls for regular opportunities for learners to speak for different purposes and audiences (NCERT 2023). Home languages can support the planning stage: learners can brainstorm and outline in Kannada, Hindi or Urdu, then present in English, and bilingual learners may present a key idea in both languages for a mixed audience.

items: Structure and signposting. Use a checklist of introduction, main points, conclusion and signposting phrases.
Delivery. Assess eye contact, pace and independence from notes, separately from language.
Question handling. Note use of clarifying, time-buying and honesty strategies in the Q&A.
Self-review. Collect learners’ recorded self-review notes and compare first and later versions.
How often do your learners speak for more than one minute without interruption?
Do your learners read from slides or scripts? What habit could you teach instead?
How do you reduce anxiety before presentations?
How do your learners handle questions after a talk?
What does useful peer feedback look like in your class?
How could you build longer, less scaffolded presentations across a year?

perm: Model presentations, slides, outlines and checklists are written for this book. Recording learners requires consent from learners and, for minors, parents or guardians; recordings should be stored securely and deleted after review. Screenshots of Google Slides, Docs, Forms, Canva, Quizlet, Mentimeter, Classroomscreen or Audacity require permission or replacement with original illustrations.
next: Coming next. Unit 41 turns to authentic materials at scale: building a course substantially around real-world texts rather than only coursebook-generated ones.

terms.def: A fluency activity in which a learner gives the same talk three times to different listeners in four, three and then two minutes, so that repetition and time pressure make speech smoother (Nation 1989).
Speech in which two or more people interact and build meaning together, as in conversation; contrast monologic speech, as in a presentation.
Extended speech produced by one speaker to an audience, such as a presentation or speech, which requires planning and organization; it differs from dialogic speech, in which speakers take turns.
Comments that learners give one another on work in progress, such as a presentation rehearsal or draft, usually guided by criteria or sentence frames.
Nervousness about speaking in front of an audience, which can hinder performance and can be reduced through rehearsal and support.

Temporary support that helps learners do what they could not yet do alone, gradually withdrawn as competence grows (Wood, Bruner and Ross 1976). Examples include sentence frames, modelling, visual prompts and guiding questions.
Learners evaluating their own performance against criteria, for example watching a phone recording of their presentation with a checklist and identifying one strength and one thing to improve.
Words and phrases that show the structure of a talk or text, such as ‘First…’, ‘Moving on to…’ and ‘To sum up…’. Speakers use them to guide listeners; listeners use them to follow the organization.
The ability to use verbal and non-verbal strategies to keep communication going when knowledge runs short, such as paraphrasing, asking for clarification or using gesture (Canale and Swain 1980).
Pictures, charts, objects, slides or board drawings used to support communication and understanding. In presentations they should support, not replace, what the speaker says.
